title: One macro, distributed by URL
description: Define a [DuckDB macro](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_macro) once — in a Git repo, gist, or any HTTP-served file — and `LOAD` it into any DuckDB session by URL. The point is **centralized, versioned macro distribution**: one source of truth for shared SQL helpers across machines, teammates, and notebooks.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: DuckDB macros are great for encapsulating reusable SQL — a normalization helper, a parameterized search, a custom aggregate pattern. The friction is **distribution**: copy-paste between notebooks, drift between machines, no version control on the SQL itself. WebMacro replaces copy-paste with a URL.

bulletPoints.label: One source of truth
bulletPoints.description: Host the macro definition where your team already collaborates — a Git repo, an internal wiki that serves raw text, an S3 bucket, a private gist. Everyone calling `load_macro_from_url` gets the same SQL.

bulletPoints.label: Version-controlled SQL
bulletPoints.description: Pin a specific commit URL (e.g. `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/repo/<sha>/macros/foo.sql`) and you've got reproducible macro loading. Reviewable in pull requests; rollback is a URL change.

bulletPoints.label: Session-start bootstrap
bulletPoints.description: Load a handful of standard macros at the top of a notebook or script — one `SELECT load_macro_from_url(url) FROM (VALUES (...))` call and the session has its toolbox.

bulletPoints.label: Both scalar and table macros
bulletPoints.description: DuckDB supports [scalar `MACRO`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_macro#scalar-macros) and [table `MACRO`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_macro#table-macros). WebMacro loads either — whatever the URL's body parses as.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: `load_macro_from_url` is a single scalar function. Internally: `GET` the URL, parse the body, create the macro, return a status string. There is no caching, no manifest, no dependency graph — it's deliberately the simplest possible primitive.

bulletPoints.label: HTTPS GET
bulletPoints.description: On DuckDB 2.0 the request goes through DuckDB's own HTTP stack, the same one `read_csv('https://...')` uses: httpfs is autoloaded for `https://`, and `http_timeout`, `http_retries`, `http_proxy` and [HTTP secrets](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/httpfs/https) (e.g. a bearer token) apply. Redirects are followed (so a `gist.github.com/...` URL that 301s to `gist.githubusercontent.com/...` works), and every hop is checked again, so an `https://` URL can't be redirected to plain `http://`. Responses larger than `webmacro_max_response_size` (default 1 MiB) are refused. The Haybarn 1.5 build uses [`cpp-httplib`](https://github.com/yhirose/cpp-httplib) with a 10 second read timeout.

bulletPoints.label: Parser validation
bulletPoints.description: The fetched body is parsed with DuckDB's own parser and must be exactly one `CREATE MACRO` or `CREATE OR REPLACE MACRO` statement. Anything else raises an error and nothing runs. On DuckDB 2.0 `TEMP` macros are allowed; the Haybarn 1.5 build rejects them because it creates the macro on a separate connection.

bulletPoints.label: Registration
bulletPoints.description: On DuckDB 2.0 the macro is created in your own transaction, exactly like running the `CREATE MACRO` statement yourself: your `search_path` decides where an unqualified macro goes, a `ROLLBACK` removes it, and read-only databases or `READ ONLY` transactions refuse it. In an in-memory database it lasts until the database closes; in a database file it stays until you drop it.

bulletPoints.label: WASM build
bulletPoints.description: In DuckDB-WASM the extension fetches with the browser's `XMLHttpRequest` — same function surface and the same URL, size and statement checks; TLS, redirects and CORS are handled by the browser.

sections.title: Trust model
sections.description: **This extension fetches and executes SQL from a URL.** Any URL you load is, in effect, code running in your DuckDB session. The trust posture below is the central caveat — read it before pointing this at anything you didn't author.

bulletPoints.label: Only load from URLs you control
bulletPoints.description: Your own Git repos, your team's internal artifact host, your own gists. Don't load from URLs found in chat messages, Stack Overflow, or random blog posts — same posture you'd use for `curl ... | bash`. See [OWASP — Code Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Code_Injection).

bulletPoints.label: The statement check is not a sandbox
bulletPoints.description: It stops a file from running anything else when it loads. It doesn't limit the macro itself: a macro's body can do whatever your session can, such as reading files or URLs, and it runs whenever you call the macro.

bulletPoints.label: Pin URLs to immutable revisions
bulletPoints.description: If you load from a Git host, prefer URLs with a commit SHA over branch names — `.../<sha>/macros/foo.sql` rather than `.../main/macros/foo.sql`. That way a compromised or rebased branch doesn't silently change what you load tomorrow.

bulletPoints.label: HTTPS only by default
bulletPoints.description: HTTPS prevents network-level tampering between your DuckDB and the macro host. On DuckDB 2.0 plain `http://` URLs are refused unless you `SET webmacro_allow_http = true` (use only for localhost or lab networks), and `load_macro_from_url` refuses to run at all when `enable_external_access` is false.

bulletPoints.label: No cross-session caching
bulletPoints.description: Every `load_macro_from_url` call hits the network. If the upstream changes, the next session sees the change. Pin URLs for reproducibility.

useCases.title: Team macro library in a Git repo
useCases.description: Keep a `macros/` directory in a shared Git repo, one `.sql` file per macro. At session start, `load_macro_from_url` the ones you need. Pull requests review macro changes; URLs pinned to a tag give you reproducible builds.

useCases.title: Reusable analyst toolbox
useCases.description: Domain-specific helpers (date bucketing for your fiscal calendar, custom string normalization, parameterized lookup macros) live at stable URLs and load at the top of every analyst notebook — no copy-paste drift.

useCases.title: Live demos and tutorials
useCases.description: Host an example macro at a stable URL; tutorials and blog posts can `load_macro_from_url` it in one line instead of pasting twenty lines of `CREATE MACRO`. Readers see the focal SQL, not the boilerplate.

useCases.title: Versioned SQL distribution to ephemeral workers
useCases.description: Short-lived workers that spin up DuckDB (Lambda, ETL containers) bootstrap their macro environment from a single trusted URL — no need to bake macro SQL into the image.
